parts.name: Retention comb — 3-gate bench segment

print.orientationWhy: Flat on the bed. The seats are the accurate feature and want no support.

parts.note: The bench slice. The full machine uses a 10-gate arc on the same pitch and the same seat.

parts.name: Gate wheel tooth

print.orientationWhy: Flat, arm in the XY plane. The bending load is in-plane, so layer lines never see peel.

parts.note: Carries one gate. Eight per wheel; the bench runs two so pickup and release can both be watched.

parts.name: Printed crochet hook — 3.0 mm nose

print.orientationWhy: Nose up, solid, 0.12 mm layers. This is the one part where surface finish is a function and not a preference — every layer line is something cotton can catch on.

parts.note: A consumable. Five per spool of filament, and the round number where one starts snagging is data worth keeping.
parts.status: Manual experiment; slice and inspect before printing

parts.name: Hook collet

print.orientationWhy: Bore axis vertical. The clamp slit must not fall on a layer boundary.

parts.note: Swapping hook nose diameter is a reprint of this and the hook — no other part moves.

parts.name: MGN9 rail bracket to 2020

print.orientationWhy: Web flat on the bed; the foot then prints as a bridge-free upstand.

parts.note: Slotted feet so the rail can be squared to the comb before lock-down.

parts.name: NEMA17 mount with thermistor pocket

print.orientationWhy: Flat. PETG not PLA here specifically because this part touches a motor that runs warm for hours.

parts.note: The thermistor pocket is a safety feature, not a convenience. Fit the sensor before first power-on.

parts.name: Camera pod

print.orientationWhy: Open side up so the aperture needs no support. PLA is fine — nothing here gets warm.

parts.note: Aimed square at the throat. The slotted clamp is how you set the ROI without moving the machine.

parts.name: Yarn tension dancer

print.orientationWhy: Flat. The arm is a beam; keep layers in-plane.

parts.note: The dancer is what turns "yarn feed" into a measurable quantity. Without it, T3 loop height is luck.

parts.name: Yarn-over finger arm

print.orientationWhy: Flat. This part reverses direction twice per stitch — keep layers out of the bending plane.

parts.note: The wire tip is 1.75 mm filament or spring steel. A printed tip at that diameter snaps within a round.

parts.name: Yarn spinner base

print.orientationWhy: Flat, bearing seat up. Print the seat last so its first layer is not the one fighting the bed.

parts.note: One 608 per spinner. You already bought four for the wheel and the dancer, so this is the cheapest subsystem on the machine.

parts.name: Yarn spinner spindle

print.orientationWhy: Fingers up, flange on the bed. Printed on its side the fingers become cantilevers across the layers and snap off the first time a skein is dropped on.

parts.note: Takes a nøste, a cake or a cone. Four sprung fingers, no adjustment, no fasteners.

parts.name: Yarn spinner guide arm

print.orientationWhy: Upright, no supports — the arm is a 46 mm overhang that bridges cleanly at this width.

parts.note: The eyelet sits above and inboard of the skein, so the strand leaves the top of the roll and never rubs the spindle.

parts.name: Bench base plate

print.orientationWhy: Flat, obviously. Slow first layer — a warped base makes every calibration lie.

parts.note: The only part of the bench rig that does not carry into the full machine. Filament, not money.

parts.name: Mandrel — crown dome

print.orientationWhy: Dome up, no supports. The inside is never seen and never touched by yarn.

parts.note: Lathed from the app’s own buildProfile() rings, so the former is the shape the pattern makes.

parts.name: Mandrel — wall section

print.orientationWhy: Open cylinder, printed as-is. Bayonets top and bottom.

parts.note: Profile selected for RO RO RO; carries its 10 chart rounds — the part of the hat the lettering lands on.

parts.name: Mandrel — brim skirt

print.orientationWhy: Largest part on the plate at 240 mm. Slow first layer — a warped brim tilts every round above it.

parts.note: Radius capped at 120 mm so it fits the plate; the fabric brim hangs past the edge, which is fine because this is a datum, not a mould.

parts.name: Turntable platter (GT2 rim groove)

print.orientationWhy: Flat. This is the concentricity datum for the whole machine — check it with a dial indicator before you trust it.

parts.note: Driven by GT2 on the rim, so the reduction is ~34:1 with no gearbox. One stitch is 8.4 motor steps.

parts.name: Hub adapter — lazy-susan to platter

print.orientationWhy: Flat, 5 walls. It carries the whole rotating mass.

parts.note: The lazy-susan bearing is BOUGHT, never printed — it sets the machine’s concentricity.

parts.name: Retention comb — 10 gates

print.orientationWhy: Flat. The seats are the accurate feature; no supports near them.

parts.note: The bench 3-gate segment scaled to 10. Same pitch, same seat, same gate part — nothing relearned.

parts.name: Gate wheel hub (8 teeth)

print.orientationWhy: Flat, bore vertical. Every tooth registers off this face.

parts.note: Takes the same 8 teeth the bench rig used two of. Nothing about the tooth changes.

parts.name: Yarn turret — 4 colours

print.orientationWhy: Flat. The four feed bores must stay parallel or the yarn rubs.

parts.note: Indexes on the SECOND yarn-over, so the colour change is locked inside the stitch. Up to 1 412 times per hat.

parts.name: Take-down skirt

print.orientationWhy: TPU, flat. The fingers must flex — printed rigid, they scar the fabric instead of tensioning it.

parts.note: Keeps finished fabric hanging clear of the gates. Without it the hat climbs back into the comb around round 20.

parts.name: Station column bracket

print.orientationWhy: Flat. Slotted to the deck so the column can be trammed vertical.

parts.note: Carries the Z column. Tram this vertical before anything above it is trusted.

parts.name: Gate socket calibration rack · R1

print.orientationWhy: Flat bottom on the plate; five sockets and index dots face up. No supports inside sockets.

parts.note: Manual fit/yarn experiment only. Five sockets with 0.15–0.55 mm total clearance; not a stitch-spacing comb and not a motorised crochet machine.
parts.status: Manual experiment; slice and inspect before printing

findings.title: Platter and hub bolt circles do not meet
findings.evidence: The actual CAD cutters put six platter holes on radius 102 mm and six hub holes on radius 53 mm: 49 mm radial mismatch. The legacy fit checks omit this pair.
findings.action: Redesign both around the selected bearing and shared bolt pattern, including a centring register, stack height and fastener engagement.

findings.title: The nominal gate quantity is short
findings.evidence: The full comb needs 10 gates and the wheel 8; the old registry supplies 12. At least 18 installed gates are needed, before spares.
findings.action: Use 18 installed + 2 spares in the provisional full-machine quote; choose the final throat only after yarn trials.

findings.title: Bench comb gate pockets are buried
findings.evidence: Even the upper pocket reaches only Z=12.24 mm inside the 14 mm tall comb. Only the small ejector holes reach the top; an 8 × 2.6 mm gate tongue cannot enter from above.
findings.action: Use the new open-top calibration rack for initial measurements. Redesign the working comb sockets before assembly.

findings.title: Hook shaft is crosswise to its insertion axis
findings.evidence: The hook shaft is modelled along local Z, then mounted with a 90-degree X rotation. Its direction is 90.0 degrees from the P insertion axis. Translating P therefore sweeps the hook sideways rather than driving the tip along its shaft.
findings.action: Redesign hook and collet together around a shared tool centreline; verify the tip path, tool closure and collision clearance through the actual stitch cycle. Do not fake this movement in an animation.

findings.title: Several intended through-holes end inside the solid
findings.evidence: bore() creates a centred cutter, while platter and hub bodies are extruded upward from Z=0. The platter cutter ends at Z=8 inside its 10 mm body; the hub cutter ends at Z=7 inside its 8 mm body. Their bolt passages retain 2 mm and 1 mm roofs. These solids still pass watertight-mesh checks.
findings.action: Retire these interfaces with the wheel design. For any reused part, test a full fastener/tool insertion path against actual CSG and measured hardware.

findings.title: A ten-stitch comb does not locate an entire round
findings.evidence: A roughly 100-stitch round exceeds the ten comb positions. V1 has no demonstrated transfer sequence that keeps each future insertion point located until the next round reaches it. A mesh or timed animation cannot fill this gap.
findings.action: Replace passive reacquisition with retained stitch positions. Prove insertion, loop formation and transfer on a short needle bed before designing circular storage.

findings.title: Hook closure and yarn retraction are missing control functions
findings.evidence: The V1 hook is permanently open. Its dancer is a passive arm; there is no measured yarn-tension loop or commanded slack take-up. Their adequacy for repeated draw-through is an untested assumption.
findings.action: Evaluate a polished metal compound tool with controlled closure and rotation, plus measured feeding/retraction. Establish tool/yarn compatibility physically before freezing dimensions.

findings.title: Existing odds and cycle times are not experimental results
findings.evidence: The prior one-percent completion figure is a product of subjective stage probabilities. Timing is programmed into a simulation. Neither is a measured chance or speed of this machine.
findings.action: Record trial counts, failure modes, actual cycle times and recovery outcomes. Report assumptions explicitly; do not use simulated timing or invented odds as a purchasing argument.

findings.title: Wheel retention and bearings need a complete design
findings.evidence: The existing tooth and wheel hub have no shared mounting contract. Shaft supports, positive torque transfer, pulley geometry and belt tensioning are not fully modelled.
findings.action: Specify bought shaft/bearings/pulleys, CAD each support and retainer, then check the swept volume against the comb.

findings.title: Linear drives and yarn-over actuator are incomplete
findings.evidence: The legacy hardware picture uses rail/motor envelopes. It does not contain a complete Z/R/P bearing, lead-nut, coupling, endstop and carriage attachment chain. The yarn finger also needs its actuator and mount.
findings.action: Freeze exact supplier drawings and model every load-bearing interface before issuing assembly instructions.

findings.title: No deployable machine controller exists
findings.evidence: HKP/1 is a protocol and simulated transport. The repository does not provide tested ESP32 motion firmware, a complete wiring drawing, homing, or an integrated detector.
findings.action: Implement and bench-test homing, travel limits, sensor faults, stop/reset behaviour and one measured stitch cycle. Size the DC power system from the selected loads.

findings.title: Automatic crochet has no physical evidence
findings.evidence: Rendered motion and watertight meshes do not demonstrate stitch capture, loop retention, draw-through, round transfer, increases or colour changes.
findings.action: Record fit trials, then a single stitch, 50 consecutive stitches, a closed round, increases, one complete single-colour hat, and finally colour changes.

findings.title: X1 Carbon selected; manufacturing profile is not qualified
findings.evidence: The owner confirmed Bambu Lab X1 Carbon. A 0.4 mm nozzle is assumed, not confirmed. Material brand, shrinkage, supports and physical fit remain unqualified. The 256 mm bed also has a front-left exclusion in its default profile.
findings.action: Slice and inspect each plate using explicit profiles and retain support-inclusive grams/time. Check fit physically before releasing mating parts. Slicing old CAD does not resolve its mechanical defects.

fitSteps.title: Slice and label the eight pieces
fitSteps.body: Use millimetres and 100% scale. Print one rack, one each of the 6 / 7 / 7.5 mm gates, two 8 mm gates, and two hooks. Mark each gate with its throat width. The hook is a finish experiment, not an established replacement for a metal hook.
fitSteps.check: Preview every layer for unsupported islands. The rack sockets face upward. Record support/brim grams and print time from the slicer.

fitSteps.title: Measure the printed fit
fitSteps.body: Remove strings without enlarging the sockets. One dot is 8.15 × 2.75 mm; each next socket increases both dimensions by 0.10 mm. All sockets are 4.2 mm deep. Try the SAME gate in all five sockets; the gate tongue is nominally 8 × 2.6 × 4 mm below its shoulder.
fitSteps.check: Record measured tongue size and the smallest socket that seats by gentle finger pressure without rocking. Do not force a press fit. This test measures fit, not stitch capture.

fitSteps.title: Secure the rack and insert a gate
fitSteps.body: Clamp the rack to a bench using soft jaws, leaving the sockets accessible. Optional mounting holes are Ø4.5 mm on a 104 × 24 mm rectangle; choose screw length for your actual backing board. Insert one gate in the selected socket. The loose fit is intentional; keep it seated by hand during the experiment.
fitSteps.check: The rack stays fixed and the gate shoulder touches its top face. No motors or electrical parts are used.

fitSteps.title: Test one yarn loop and one draw-through
fitSteps.body: Use a hand-crocheted swatch of the intended yarn. Manually place one stitch in an 8 mm gate; guide the hook through while holding the fabric. Try a yarn-over and draw-through by hand. Narrower gates are comparison samples: the existing 3 mm hook + two 2.1 mm yarn legs + 0.6 mm margin require 7.8 mm, so narrower variants are not expected to pass that assumed stack.
fitSteps.check: Record snagging, loop escape, splits, hook damage, yarn and hook measurements. Stop if yarn frays or the hook bends. Successful manual manipulation does not establish automatic crochet.

fitSteps.title: Record the comparison results
fitSteps.body: Save printer model, nozzle, material, slicer profile, project file, grams, time, the fit measurements and a close-up video of the experiment. Repeat on at least 50 loops, recording failures rather than changing the result after the fact.
fitSteps.check: These results characterise the old gate concept only. They do not qualify the selected metal-tool, retained-stitch replacement. Follow the critical review for that development sequence.

redesign.status: Selected direction for experiments; complete-machine CAD not frozen
redesign.decision: Retire the gate-wheel mechanism as the main development path. Build a constrained-stitch test platform with retained stitch positions, a controlled metal tool and measured yarn tension.
redesign.target: Keep a true-crochet, seamless bucket hat as the final target. A small flat swatch is an experiment toward that target, not a substituted finished product. A panel-and-seam route is an alternative only if acceptable to the owner.
redesign.reasoning: The dominant risk is loss of control over the yarn and stitch position, not how many parts fit on a printer. Spending time completing the old frame would lock us into its weakest assumption. First establish a repeatable stitch process, then design the geometry that carries it around the hat.

evidence.name: CroMat doctoral research · Storck, 2024
evidence.finding: Paired auxiliary needles retain the fabric. The tool has controlled shaft/slider motion and rotation. Printed auxiliary bars were rejected after friction and bending problems. The documented prototype uses ten axes; its trials do not validate our DK-cotton hat.
evidence.location: Sections 3.1.4–3.1.5 and 3.4; printed pp. 52–56, 89–94, 100–101. Full text inspected.
evidence.implication: Use this as a mechanism reference, not as a drop-in ten-axis parts list or a promise that a simpler clone will work.

evidence.name: Machine-producible crochet patterns · Storck et al., 2023
evidence.finding: The flat-bed process has specific shaping limits, including where increases and decreases can occur. Circular hand patterns cannot simply be sent to a flat-bed controller.
evidence.location: Introduction and pp. 265–267; paper and stitch-topology figure inspected.
evidence.implication: A panel-built hat needs a separate pattern compiler and changes the construction. It is not silently interchangeable with the current hat.

evidence.name: Active low-cost thread tensioning · Kellner et al., 2025
evidence.finding: This CroMat project describes active feeding/retraction with a storage spring and load-cell feedback.
evidence.location: Author conference abstract, published 3 December 2025. Not a production reliability report.
evidence.implication: Measure tension through the whole stitch cycle and design slack management explicitly.

evidence.name: Loom-Based Mechanized Crochet · Smith et al., 2026
evidence.finding: The published abstract describes a robotic tool acting on a constrained fabric matrix.
evidence.location: Abstract only; SCF 2025 event, publication dated 18 February 2026. Full method and performance not verified.
evidence.implication: Additional support for investigating constrained fabric. No conclusion about affordable home-scale hat production follows from this abstract.

options.name: Gate wheel + ten-gate comb
options.evidence: Existing CAD only; no successful yarn trials.
options.why: Passive stitch reacquisition, unclosed hook and missing retention/drive details compound each other.

options.name: Paired-needle flat test bed
options.evidence: Demonstrated mechanism family in CroMat; our implementation remains unbuilt.
options.fit: Strong platform for studying insertion, draw-through and transfer.
options.why: Makes yarn ownership observable and lets us test one operation at a time. Full tool sourcing and gauge adaptation remain necessary.

options.name: Retained-stitch circular carrier
options.evidence: Engineering proposal; circular transfer/increases not demonstrated here.
options.why: Every required stitch must stay indexed. Small crown radius, variable stitch count, transfer and removal need separate solutions.

options.name: Flat panels, joined into a hat
options.evidence: Flat shaped crochet is documented; this hat pattern is not implemented.
options.why: Avoids circular carrier development, but needs shaped-panel pattern conversion, joining instructions and acceptance of the changed hat.

modules.name: Stitch storage
modules.action: An exchangeable bed of paired metal holders; start with only enough positions to prove neighbouring-stitch transfer.
modules.make: Print housing and adjustment fixtures; buy precision yarn-contact elements.
modules.open: Exact needle SKU, gauge, stroke, clearance and yarn compatibility.

modules.name: Working tool
modules.action: Separate insertion, rotation and hook-closure functions. Track where each loop sits during each motion.
modules.make: Buy polished metal tool and slider; print noncritical housings.
modules.open: Available compound tool or equivalent controlled closure; tool supplier drawing.

modules.name: Yarn system
modules.action: Measure tension, feed yarn and take back slack. Start with one colour and one measured yarn.
modules.make: Buy ceramic guides, sensor, bearings and motor; print guides/housings.
modules.open: Required tension range, sensor resolution, feed travel and response time.

modules.name: Fabric control
modules.action: Defined cast-off edges and adjustable take-down keep the work in the working plane.
modules.make: Smooth bought or machined contact surfaces; printed mounts.
modules.open: Forces, edge geometry, clearance during transfer and finished-fabric removal.

modules.name: Motion and frame
modules.action: Use supplier-dimensioned rails/stages. Choose axis count from the proven stitch sequence.
modules.make: Metal load paths and guides; printed brackets where tolerances permit.
modules.open: No axis count, torque, speed or full frame size is released yet.

modules.name: Controller and recovery
modules.action: Local motion limits and stop chain. Verify transfers before advancing; stop for ambiguous state.
modules.make: Standard controller/driver platform and documented harness.
modules.open: Controller capacity, wiring, fault response and recovery tests; no deployable firmware exists yet.

milestones.title: Characterise the actual yarn and tool
milestones.deliverable: Measured yarn/hook dimensions, gauge swatch, available tool drawing and printer profile.
milestones.pass: A supplier-backed tool and clearances compatible with the intended yarn; no reliance on nominal yarn diameter alone.

milestones.title: Manual retained-stitch cell
milestones.deliverable: Dimensioned fixture, clamp/holder detail and video of the complete stitch and retention transfer.
milestones.pass: One true single crochet repeatedly completed with traceable loop ownership; record all failures and forces. Operator performs unmotorised motions.

milestones.title: Powered cell and neighbouring stitches
milestones.deliverable: All mating parts, wiring, homing, tool closure, tension feedback, firmware and an operation log.
milestones.pass: At least 50 consecutive stitches as an initial development gate, then multiple rows with no manual loop placement between stitches. This is not production qualification.

milestones.title: Faults and longer runs
milestones.deliverable: Tests for loop loss, snagging, yarn break, stalled motion, sensor failure and restart.
milestones.pass: Safe, observable stop with the last verified state retained; sustained run and material-change tests. Report per-operation failure/recovery rates.

milestones.title: Choose and prove the hat transport
milestones.deliverable: Circular retained-stitch transfer prototype, or separately accepted shaped-panel plan.
milestones.pass: For seamless hats: complete rounds, round transitions, increases and removal are physically demonstrated before full CAD release.

milestones.title: Full manufacturing release
milestones.deliverable: Complete native CAD and exchange models, every fastener/shaft/guard, tolerance drawings, purchased SKUs, verified plate profiles, final quote and illustrated assembly/wiring guide.
milestones.pass: A physical single-colour hat passes the chosen dimensions and stitch checks. Add multicolour operation only after reliable yarn selection and strand control.

legacySteps.title: Print the catch test — nothing else yet
G0 — does a gate catch a live stitch?
G2 — the wheel takes it out of the comb
